findings.title: The crop dimension assertion runs AFTER the object is already written to production R2
findings.description: In `backfillCrops` the `PutObjectCommand` (411-419) is sent before the width/height check (424-429). The comment on that check says "Object NOT trusted" and it throws — but by then the re-encoded bytes are already at the live key. The catch at 446 records the item as `failed`, the run exits 1, and the operator is told the object was not trusted, while production is serving it. Worse, the failure path never records the item in `purgeUrls` (only `status === 'rewritten'` entries are collected at 506/527), so the one object that IS known to be wrong is the one object that will never be purged from the Cloudflare edge — and it is served `immutable` for a year with no undo of the prior bytes.
findings.fix: Move the `encoded.width !== meta.width || encoded.height !== meta.height` check to immediately after `encodeUnderCeiling` returns and before the `PutObjectCommand` is sent, so a dimension change aborts the item without writing anything.

findings.title: The undo file — the only record of the irreversible crop rewrites — is written once, at the very end
findings.description: `writeFileSync(args.undo, …)` runs after BOTH phases complete. Phase `crops` replaces bytes at an existing key with no backup of the prior object (the header admits recovery means re-cutting through Rekognition), and those URLs are `immutable` for a year, so the undo file's `purgeUrls` list is the only thing that makes the change visible at the edge and the only record of what was touched. Any interruption after the first crop PUT — Ctrl-C, a dropped Postgres connection during phase `variants` (which runs first under `--phase all` and would abort before crops even start), an OOM in sharp, a network fault — leaves production with rewritten bytes, a stale Cloudflare edge, and zero record of which of the 309 crops were rewritten. Compounding this, `args.undo` is only checked for presence (469-472), never for writability: a path whose directory does not exist passes the guard, both phases run to completion against production, and then `writeFileSync` throws ENOENT into the top-level catch — every purge URL and every reversal id lost after the writes have already landed.
findings.fix: Pre-flight the undo path before any write (write a stub `{}` to it at startup, after arg parsing, and fail with exit 2 if that throws), and append each outcome to the file incrementally — flush after every completed item, or at minimum after each phase — so an interrupted run still yields the purge list and the reversal ids.

findings.title: A crop whose HEAD fails or 404s is silently counted as under the ceiling and the run exits 0
findings.description: `sized` does `fetch(c.url, { method: 'HEAD' })` and never checks `res.ok`; a throw is swallowed by the bare `catch` and yields `bytes: 0`. A 404 (a crop object that does not exist, e.g. an article whose `?v=` token moved), a 5xx from the edge, a DNS blip or a transient TCP reset therefore all produce `bytes: 0`. Line 360 then filters that item OUT of `over` because `0 > 300000` is false; line 361 excludes it from `totalOver`; it never appears in `crops`, never in `failedC`, and never in the `bad` sum at 598. The run prints a smaller over-ceiling count than reality and exits 0 — the exit code that the ship gate reads as 'the backfill is complete'. With 408 HEADs fired at concurrency 8 against a CDN, a handful of transient failures is the expected case, not the exotic one.
findings.fix: Return an explicit `ok` flag from the sizing pass (`ok: res.ok`), and treat every `!ok` candidate as a hard failure: emit it as a `CropOutcome` with `status: 'failed'` so it lands in `failedC` and forces exit 1, rather than letting it fall through the ceiling filter as if it measured zero bytes.

findings.title: The named pre-ship gate cannot detect the 404 disaster it is documented to guard against
findings.description: `backfill-image-mid.mts:22` and `article-image-variant.ts:18-21` both state the safety order as: run the backfill against production, confirm this audit reports zero misses, then ship. That gate cannot work. The audit measures URLs scraped from RENDERED production HTML (123-133), and until the render change deploys those pages emit `high.webp` — the audit never requests a single `mid.webp` URL, so it can never prove `mid` coverage before the deploy. (It will also fail outright pre-deploy, because the `high` files it does measure are the 174 over 500,000 B that motivated the change.) Coverage is a second, unreconciled problem: the backfill enumerates `media` rows matching `variants ? 'high'` (224), while the renderer rewrites every body-figure URL found in article content. Any figure whose URL ends `/high.webp` or `/original.{ext}` but whose media row is absent, or carries the R2 object without the `high` key in its JSONB (13 of the 1,087 rows carry no `high` at all), gets no `mid.webp` written and 404s the instant the render change goes live. Nothing in the change reconciles the set of URLs in article content against the set of rows the backfill visits.
findings.fix: Add a coverage check that runs against the DATA, not the rendered page, before the deploy: enumerate every `/high.webp` and `/original.*` URL in `articles` Tiptap content, rewrite each to `mid.webp` with `getArticleVariantUrl`, HEAD it, and fail on any miss. Alternatively run the existing audit with `--base` pointed at a preview deployment that already carries the render change, and say so in the header instead of naming production.

findings.title: A crop still over the ceiling exits 0 whenever the re-encode did not come out smaller
findings.description: The `bad` sum counts `overC`, which is `rewritten.filter(c => c.overCeiling)` (558). But a crop that runs the whole ladder to q45, is still over 300,000 B, and encodes no smaller than the file already there hits the `encoded.bytes >= c.bytes` guard at 399 and returns `status: 'skipped'`. Skipped items are in neither `rewritten` nor `failedC`, so they contribute nothing to `bad`. The run therefore prints its over-ceiling census, leaves those crops over budget on production, and exits 0 — telling the ship gate the ceiling is met when it is not. This is precisely the population the whole crops phase exists for: the worst-entropy photographs (`songket-tenunan-tangan-atau-cetak` at 1,430 KB is named in `CROP_CEILING`'s own comment).
findings.fix: Carry `overCeiling` on the skipped-because-not-smaller outcome and include skipped-but-still-over-ceiling crops in the `bad` arithmetic, so any crop left above `CROP_CEILING.CEILING_BYTES` forces a non-zero exit.

findings.title: A non-numeric --concurrency makes the pool run zero workers and the script reports total success
findings.description: `num()` returns `Number(v)`, so `--concurrency abc` yields `NaN`. `?? 4` does not catch it (NaN is not nullish). In `pooled`, `Math.max(1, NaN)` is `NaN`, `Array.from({ length: NaN }, worker)` is `[]`, and `Promise.all([])` resolves immediately, leaving `out` as a SPARSE array of holes. `Array.prototype.filter` skips holes, so `written`, `failedV`, `rewritten` and `failedC` are all empty, `bad` is 0, and the script prints 'variants written 0 failed 0 / crops rewritten 0 failed 0' followed by EXIT 0 — indistinguishable from a run that had nothing left to do. An operator who fat-fingers the flag gets a green backfill that wrote nothing, then ships the render change on the strength of it. Verified in Node: `Array.from({length: Math.max(1, NaN)})` has length 0 and a 3-hole sparse array filters to length 0.
findings.fix: Validate every numeric argument at parse time — reject with exit 2 when `Number.isFinite` is false for `--concurrency`, `--sleep-ms` or `--limit` — and make `pooled` throw rather than silently spawn zero workers when `concurrency` is not a positive integer.

findings.title: The crops phase hardcodes the inspire bucket where the writer resolves the bucket per key
findings.description: `backfillCrops` reads and writes with `bucket = getR2Bucket()` (passed in from main:478), but `generateSmartCrops` — the code that PUT these objects — picks its bucket with `resolveR2Bucket(originalKey)` (smart-crop.ts:484-489), which routes any key not starting with `inspire/` to `getR2AssetsBucket()`. Any cover outside the `inspire/` namespace therefore has its crops in the assets bucket, the `GetObjectCommand` at 139 raises NoSuchKey, and that crop can never be brought under the ceiling by this script — it just fails, counts into `failedC`, and forces exit 1 with no route to a green run.
findings.fix: Resolve the bucket per crop key the same way the writer does — export or duplicate `resolveR2Bucket` and select the bucket from `extractKeyFromUrl(c.url)` — rather than assuming every crop lives in `R2_BUCKET_NAME`.

findings.title: Re-running the crops phase stacks generational loss on the crops that need it most, with no undo
findings.description: The skip predicate is `bytes > CEILING_BYTES`, so a crop that finishes still over 300 KB is re-selected by the next run. That run re-encodes it from the ALREADY degraded stored bytes, starting again at rung 0 (q100) and walking down — a second full lossy generation on the same pixels, then a third. Because the run exits 1 whenever such a crop exists (598-602), the operator is actively invited to re-run. `--force` is the same problem across the whole corpus: it re-encodes all 408 crops from their stored WebP, and a q100 recompression of an already-compressed WebP is usually slightly SMALLER, so the `encoded.bytes >= c.bytes` guard at 399 will not stop it — every crop on the site silently picks up a second generation with no backup of the prior bytes. Two concurrent runs produce the same stacking by racing each other's PUTs.
findings.fix: Record the achieved quality (or a marker key/object metadata) so a crop that already ran the full ladder is skipped on a re-run rather than re-encoded from its own output, and re-encode `--force` items from the ORIGINAL via `processSmartCrops` geometry rather than from the stored crop.

findings.title: getDefaultPresets merges only at the preset-name level, so a partial `mid` row still breaks generation
findings.description: `{ ...DEFAULT_PRESETS, ...(row[0].value) }` is a shallow spread: it protects a MISSING `mid` key, which is what the doc comment claims, but an admin row containing `mid: { quality: 90 }` with no `maxWidth` replaces the default object wholesale and leaves `maxWidth` undefined. `generateVariants` then calls `.resize({ width: undefined, withoutEnlargement: true })`, which sharp treats as no resize at all — so `mid.webp` is generated at the source's full width (up to 2400+) and the `MID_PRESET` ladder grinds quality down to 30 trying to fit 350 KB, producing exactly the oversized-and-ugly body figure the change exists to remove. The same hole applies to a partial `low` or `high`.
findings.fix: Merge per preset, not per name: `mid: { ...DEFAULT_PRESETS.mid, ...row.mid }` for each key (or validate the row's shape and drop any preset missing `quality` or `maxWidth` back to the default).

findings.title: Cover renditions are now derived from a possibly stepped-down crop buffer
findings.description: `renderCoverRendition(croppedBuffer, spec)` is fed `cropped.buffer`, which since this change may be a q45 output rather than the q100 it was always given before. For the crops that actually trip `CROP_CEILING` — the high-entropy photographs the ceiling exists for — every `COVER_RENDITIONS` rung (`-sm`/`-md`) is now a resize of an already heavily-compressed image and then a second lossy encode on top, so the `.s-row` and article-cover renditions for exactly those covers degrade visibly. The diff's comment argues only that an UNDER-ceiling crop is byte-identical to before; it does not mention that the over-ceiling case changes the input to the rendition loop.
findings.fix: Keep a rung-0 (q100) buffer from the extract/resize pipeline for the rendition loop to consume, and use the ceiling-constrained buffer only for the `crop-*.webp` object that is actually served at that size.
